answer: Helium is a 7‑billion‑parameter text‑only language model that was pretrained on 2.1 trillion tokens of public English data. [1]

Inner Monologue is a method that decomposes speech into a chain of text, semantic and acoustic tokens and predicts this structured sequence in a hierarchical manner, allowing the same utterance to be represented as both text and speech without switching modalities [1]. It is used because integrating acoustic tokens into the generative model enables generating arbitrary voices and conditions rather than a single speaker, and the hierarchical modeling lets Moshi decompose the generation task without increasing the Transformer sequence length, unlike Chain‑of‑Modality [1]. Additionally, Inner Monologue predicts on a per‑frame basis, so each prediction step outputs a speech frame, making Moshi compatible with real‑time generation and enabling streaming TTS and ASR systems when combined with a delay between token types [1]. This method also significantly improves the linguistic quality of generated speech and provides streaming speech recognition and text‑to‑speech capabilities, achieving a theoretical latency of 160 ms and 200 ms in practice for a real‑time full‑duplex spoken large language model [2].
Moshi’s Helium model uses rotation positional embeddings (RoPE) [1]. The original Transformer architecture injects positional information with fixed sinusoidal encodings [2].

The ratio loss is introduced to prevent the model from converging to trivial compression behaviors, such as keeping almost all vectors or compressing too aggressively, by guiding the network toward a target compression ratio [1]. It does this by comparing the fraction of vectors actually selected (𝐹) with the average boundary probability (𝐺), which provides continuous feedback even though 𝐹 is not differentiable [1]. When 𝐹 equals 𝐺, the loss reaches its minimum, encouraging the model to match the desired ratio set by the hyperparameter 𝑁 [1]. Combined with the autoregressive prediction loss, the ratio loss preserves content‑adaptive compression, allowing the model to learn which vectors to retain based on semantic importance rather than following predetermined patterns [2].
